records.title: UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI
passages: At the fourth UNESCO forum in Riyadh, I listened to how countries and organisations were putting AI ethics into practice. I left thinking about who is accountable once AI starts shaping real decisions.

I went to the fourth UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI expecting something closer to LEAP. I thought I would spend most of the day seeing what the latest tools could do. Instead, I listened to people from governments, international organisations, research and industry work through what should happen when those tools are put to use. It was the first edition of the forum held in the Gulf. UNESCO reported more than 10,000 participants and delegations from over 50 Member States across the event in Riyadh.

The question I kept coming back to was who has to answer when AI causes harm. Think of a company using software to screen applicants. If the software rejects someone unfairly, the company needs to know who can explain what happened, who can review the decision and who can put it right. The answers get more complicated when the company, the vendor and the people affected are in different countries. The forum made the practical side of human oversight easier for me to see.

I learned more about UNESCO’s 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It gives countries a shared framework for issues such as privacy, transparency, human oversight and fair treatment. One development at the forum was RAM 2.0, an updated readiness assessment that helps countries identify gaps in their laws, institutions and technical capacity. UNESCO also released a synthesis of 55 country reports. These tools made it easier to see how governments can turn a broad commitment into work they can actually measure.

I had mostly thought about AI ethics through the decisions a system makes about people. The environmental discussions gave me another set of questions to consider. Scaling AI can put pressure on electricity, water and other resources, and those costs also have to be part of decisions about deployment. UNESCO launched a toolkit at the forum to help policymakers account for those impacts.

I spoke with people from different countries and backgrounds between sessions. Those conversations helped me understand why a shared framework can matter even when countries have different priorities. Some are deciding how to supervise systems they already rely on. Others are still building the institutions and skills they would need to do that. Hearing how people approached those questions was one of the most memorable parts of the day.

My interest in corporate law gave me another way into the discussion. When a business brings an AI system into its operations, there are questions about what data the vendor can use, who can investigate a problem and what the company has agreed to do when something goes wrong. I left wanting to understand how businesses and governments turn ethical commitments into decisions people can review and challenge.

records.title: Lead & Influence: Negotiation and Communication Workshop
passages: I completed the two-day Essentials Workshop, practising public speaking and negotiation through exercises and simulations.

I took NY Empire Academy’s two-day Essentials Workshop with Nicholas Coburn-Palo, a preceptor in public speaking at Harvard University, and Kate Clark. The format gave me time to practise both delivering a clear message and listening carefully to the person across the table.
The speaking exercises gave me a chance to organise my points before delivering them. I practised making the main point clear and giving the listener enough context to follow it.
In the simulations I practised explaining my position and listening for the other side’s priorities. Hearing what mattered to them helped me think about which parts of a proposal had room to move.

records.title: Graduation ceremony volunteering
passages: I helped set up the ceremony, seat guests and support backstage logistics as a student volunteer.

I volunteered at Al-Rowad International Schools’ graduation ceremony in May 2025. I worked alongside staff and other students, helping prepare the event space, guiding guests to their seats and lending a hand backstage.
I helped with setup before guests arrived. Once people began coming in, I guided attendees to their seats so they could get settled before the ceremony started.

I also supported the backstage team as the ceremony got underway. Working between the guest area and backstage showed me how much a smooth event depends on people keeping each other informed and picking up small tasks as they come up.

records.title: Money20/20 Middle East
passages: I explored agentic commerce and how a company can tell whether an AI agent has permission to make a purchase for someone.

Money20/20 brought banks, fintech companies and technology providers together in Riyadh. I went to see how the AI systems I had been following were being used in financial services. I attended a session on agentic commerce and walked through the exhibition, where payment companies and identity and security providers were working on different parts of the same problem.

An AI agent that can make a purchase still needs a way to prove who it represents and what it is allowed to do. The discussions about moving from pilots to live products made clear how much depends on authentication, reliable infrastructure and the controls available to the customer.

records.title: LEAP Riyadh
passages: I saw robots, autonomous delivery vehicles and palm-based payments demonstrated, and considered what it would take to use them every day.

LEAP’s 2026 edition brought startups, established technology companies and investors to Riyadh. I spent time with the exhibits on robotics, autonomous transport and new ways to pay. I also tried an F1 simulator and learned about the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.

Seeing the demonstrations gave me a better sense of what is already being tested. It also made me think about what everyday use would demand. A driverless delivery vehicle has to handle changing streets and unexpected obstacles, and a palm payment system has to protect the biometric data that makes it work.

records.title: Black Hat Middle East & Africa
passages: I attended cybersecurity workshops and briefings in Riyadh and completed ten hours of continuing professional development.

Black Hat MEA brought security researchers, practitioners and technology providers together for workshops and briefings. I joined sessions on emerging threats and approaches to defending systems. I completed ten hours of CPD activities and received a certificate for ten CPD credits.

The workshops helped me see how a team goes from understanding a threat to deciding what it can do about it. The discussions also gave me a clearer picture of how security affects decisions across an organisation, from the tools people use to how they respond when something goes wrong.

records.title: Global Airports Forum
passages: I spoke with aviation professionals about airport operations and acquired a metal collectible from a retired Emirates Airbus A380.

The forum brought airport operators, technology providers and aviation professionals to Riyadh. I met people working across different parts of the industry and heard how they manage airport operations. A short boarding delay offered a useful example. It can affect gate availability, baggage handling and the aircraft’s next flight, so several teams may need to adjust their plans together.

I became interested in how airports can use AI to anticipate delays and manage passenger flow. A prediction is useful when the teams involved can act on it, and the forum helped me see how much coordination sits behind decisions that look simple from the terminal.

I also acquired a metal collectible cut from the vertical stabiliser of a retired Emirates Airbus A380. The vertical stabiliser is the upright part of the tail. It was striking to hold a piece of an aircraft that size and know exactly where on the airframe it came from.

records.title: The Eleventh Rehearsal
passages: The voice on the tape is his. So why does the story sound rehearsed?
I’m an avid reader and I write fiction. This novel lets me explore how much of what we remember comes from stories we’ve heard over and over.

Daniel Vane edits sound for a living. He knows how much can disappear in four seconds, and how easy it is to leave a sentence that sounds whole. For seventeen years, he’s lived with a version of the night his mother vanished that has always seemed complete.

Then a file arrives from Bellwether, the country house where she worked. There’s an appointment he never agreed to and a recording he doesn’t remember making. He recognises his own voice. It’s the pause before he speaks that unnerves him.

Back in Mereford, Daniel starts to compare what he remembers with what other people kept. A voice has been edited. A photograph has changed. And the people offering to help him remember seem remarkably sure what he ought to say. Before he can work out what happened that night, he has to ask a harder question: who taught him how to tell it?
